description: Why synonyms and antonyms decide 11+ English papers, how they are tested, and a practice method that works in ten minutes a day.

sections.heading: The question type that decides papers
paragraphs: More 11+ English marks turn on synonyms and antonyms than on any other single skill. The format looks easy, which is exactly why children lose marks to it: they skim, trust recognition, and choose the word they have seen rather than the word that means the same.

Under time pressure the failure mode is consistent. A child knows the word in isolation but has never met it doing a job in a sentence, so a near-miss option that feels familiar wins over the right answer.

sections.heading: How they are actually tested
paragraphs: Typically four options, one correct, with distractors chosen to catch partial knowledge: a word that sounds similar, a word from the same topic with a different meaning, and a word the child half-remembers from somewhere else.
Gap-fill questions test the same knowledge from the other side: the word must fit the sentence, which punishes memorised definitions and rewards words met in context. This is why lists alone stall.

sections.heading: Pairs, not lists
paragraphs: Teach synonyms in pairs, never as columns. Take reluctant: pair it with unwilling, oppose it with eager, and the child has a small structure instead of a fact. Structures survive exam pressure; facts do not.
Make each new word earn its opposite before tea. It takes a minute, and it builds antonym skill as a side effect of synonym practice.

sections.heading: A ten-minute method
paragraphs: Twenty quick multiple-choice questions, same time daily, then stop, even mid-flow. Stopping early is what brings the child back tomorrow, and the words missed today show exactly what to revisit in a few days.
Follow each round into a sentence. Ask the child to use one new word at dinner or spot it in a book. A word met doing a job in a sentence survives four options under a timer.

standfirst: Synonym and antonym questions look easy, which is why they cost so many marks. They test whether a child knows a word well enough to reject three impostors in seconds.
title: Synonyms and Antonyms: the 11+ Deciders
